subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Antenatal care is systematic health monitoring from conception to labour, aiming to optimise maternal and fetal outcomes, detect complications early, and prepare for safe delivery.

sections.p: Antenatal care (ANC) is the scheduled series of clinical visits, investigations and education for a pregnant woman from conception until labour onset.
b: First visit confirms pregnancy by urine hCG or serum β‑hCG and estimates gestational age by LMP or ultrasound.

t.b: Confirms pregnancy; positive indicates gestational sac presence.
Estimates gestational age, confirms viability, detects multiple gestation or early ectopic.

sections.p: Risk is stratified into low, moderate or high based on maternal history, obstetric history and early findings.
b: High‑risk factors: previous pre‑eclampsia, diabetes, HIV, TB, anemia, multiple gestation, maternal age <18 or >35.

sections.p: Complications arise from maternal medical disease, obstetric conditions, infections and socio‑environmental factors.
b: Maternal anemia (iron deficiency, malaria, hookworm).
Infections: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, urinary tract infection, malaria.
Chronic disease: hypertension, diabetes, sickle cell disease.
Obstetric: multiple pregnancy, placenta previa, cervical insufficiency.

sections.p: Most women are asymptomatic; ANC uncovers subtle signs such as hypertension, proteinuria, anemia, or abnormal fetal growth.
b: Elevated blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks suggests pre‑eclampsia.
Hemoglobin <11 g/dL indicates anemia.
Fundal height discordance >2 cm signals growth restriction or multiple gestation.

sections.p: Investigations are chosen to screen for common maternal and fetal risks, especially in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects anemia; low values require iron/antimalarial therapy.
Identifies Rh‑negative mothers; guides anti‑D immunoglobulin administration.
Screens for congenital syphilis; positive requires penicillin treatment.
Detects maternal HIV; positive leads to ART to reduce vertical transmission.
Screens for pre‑eclampsia and gestational diabetes; abnormal results trigger further testing.
Assesses fetal viability, number, position, and growth; if unavailable, use fundal height and LMP.

sections.p: Certain findings demand urgent referral to prevent maternal or fetal loss.
b: Severe hypertension (≥160/110 mmHg) or sudden rise in BP.
Heavy vaginal bleeding or abruptio placentae signs.
Persistent severe abdominal pain with guarding.
Fetal heart rate absent on Doppler.

sections.p: Management combines preventive measures, treatment of identified conditions, and regular monitoring.
b: Iron‑folate supplementation to prevent anemia; folic acid reduces neural‑tube defects.
Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria (IPTp) with sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine in endemic areas.
Tetanus toxoid immunisation (2 doses) to prevent neonatal tetanus.
Antiretroviral therapy for HIV‑positive mothers to lower transmission risk.
Low‑dose aspirin for high‑risk pre‑eclampsia (if indicated).

sections.p: Scheduled visits every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks to 36 weeks, then weekly until delivery; each visit repeats key screens and reinforces education.
b: Counselling on nutrition, danger signs, birth planning, and breastfeeding.
Screen for gestational diabetes at 24‑28 weeks with oral glucose tolerance test where feasible.

sections.p: Antenatal care is sometimes mistaken for post‑natal care or routine obstetric check‑ups without risk assessment.
b: Post‑natal care focuses on mother and newborn after delivery, not on fetal monitoring.
Routine obstetric visits without systematic screening miss early detection of complications.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Urine dipstick protein can be false‑negative in dilute urine; confirm with 24‑hour collection if suspicion persists.
Hemoglobin may appear normal in early iron deficiency; consider ferritin if anemia risk is high.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension (≥160/110 mmHg) or sudden rise in blood pressure.
Heavy vaginal bleeding or signs of placental abruption.
Severe abdominal pain with guarding or fever.

faq.q: Why is iron‑folate given to all pregnant women?
faq.a: Pregnancy increases iron demand and folate prevents neural‑tube defects; supplementation reduces anemia and related complications.

faq.q: What is the purpose of IPTp in malaria‑endemic areas?
faq.a: Intermittent preventive treatment reduces maternal malaria episodes and prevents placental infection, improving birth weight and survival.

faq.q: How often should antenatal visits occur?
faq.a: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks to 36 weeks, then weekly until delivery.

exam: List five core components of routine antenatal care and explain their clinical importance.
Describe how you would screen for and manage anemia in a pregnant woman in a low‑resource setting.
Explain the risk‑based schedule for antenatal visits and how it changes for a high‑risk pregnancy.
